name: Notre Dame Ethics and the Common Good: AI, Work and Human Dignity
title: Notre Dame Ethics and the Common Good: AI, Work and Human Dignity
answer: The Institute for Ethics and the Common Good at the University of Notre Dame publishes news and research on artificial intelligence, much of it through its Notre Dame-IBM Technology Ethics Lab. Its most useful contribution for faith organisations is a normative framework that judges workplace AI by human dignity, drawing on Catholic social teaching from Laborem Exercens to the Vatican's 2025 Antiqua et Nova, alongside empirical work on AI exposure, hiring and labour policy.

sections.body: This is the news and research section of ethics.nd.edu, published by the Institute for Ethics and the Common Good at the University of Notre Dame, part of the Notre Dame Ethics Initiative. The material read includes blog posts from the Notre Dame-IBM Technology Ethics Lab's series AI and the Future of Work, a 2025 technology roundup, funded research write-ups, and news reports on workshops and faculty conversations. The pages carry no single publication date beyond references to events in 2025 and one workshop held on March 11.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: The site's AI content falls into three strands. The first is explanatory: posts define AI as a broad range of techniques rather than a single technology, distinguish narrow from general AI, and note that generative and agentic systems are built on older methods such as rule-based systems, machine learning and optimisation, some of which remain more reliable and interpretable for specific tasks. The second is empirical, covering labour markets. One post argues the unit of analysis should be tasks inside jobs rather than occupations, that exposure is not destiny, and that observed effects so far look like uneven augmentation rather than aggregate job loss. A Washington workshop reported that nearly a quarter of workers use generative AI weekly and 10 percent daily, with roughly one to five percent of all US work hours now AI-assisted. The third strand is normative. The final post in the AI and the Future of Work series builds a framework from Kant's distinction between price and dignity, John Paul II's Laborem Exercens, the Vatican's 2025 Antiqua et Nova, Pope Francis's 2024 World Day of Peace message, Pope Leo XIV's 2025 address to the College of Cardinals and the capabilities approach of Sen and Nussbaum.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: The roundup reports OpenAI's GPT-5 launch in August with prompts up to 400K tokens, a $500 billion OpenAI valuation, signing bonuses up to $100 million, and around $400 billion of planned 2025 AI infrastructure spending by Google, Meta, Amazon and Microsoft. It notes the open-weight performance gap shrinking from 8 percent to under 2 percent in a year, Waymo logging over 150,000 autonomous rides weekly, and EU AI Act bans on social scoring and real-time biometric surveillance effective early 2025. The workshop reports that nearly a quarter of workers use generative AI weekly and 10 percent daily, and that one to five percent of US work hours are AI-assisted. The dignity post quotes Antiqua et Nova warning AI can deskill workers and subject them to automated surveillance.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: For churches and faith organisations, this source supplies something most AI coverage does not: an explicitly theological and ethical framework for evaluating workplace AI, assembled from magisterial documents and philosophical traditions the sector already recognises. The dignity post gives leaders a vocabulary of price versus dignity, subjective versus objective work, and capability to work as a human being, which can be applied to decisions about algorithmic management, hiring tools and surveillance. The empirical posts on task exposure and augmentation help congregations and denominational employers assess claims about AI-driven job loss without either dismissing or inflating them.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Churches and Faith Organisations

sections.body: The material is a university news and blog output rather than a formal report, and several posts are parts of a series rather than standalone studies. The empirical findings are largely drawn from other researchers' work, including a Harvard survey and an International Labour Organization index, and one page is truncated mid-sentence. The content addresses AI in work, hiring and evaluation generally, not religious institutions specifically, so any application to churches and faith organisations is by extension rather than direct treatment.
sections.heading: Limits of this source
